- If sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) and model forecast is rising steadily, reduce forecast slope to avoid over-optimism.  
- If sentiment is bearish (≤0.33) and model forecast is flat or rising, apply downward bias to reflect pessimism.  
- After a sharp spike in price (e.g., >10% from prior day), model tends to overshoot — cap forecast growth to 3–5% per day post-spike.  
- When supply net is negative and bullish sentiment is low, model often underestimates downside — add 2–4% buffer below forecast for 3–5 days.  
- If recent auction events are frequent (e.g., 3+ per 30d), model overreacts to short-term volatility — smooth 30d forecast with 5-day moving average.  
- If sentiment history shows alternating bullish/bearish cycles, model tends to lag — adjust forecast to align with sentiment peaks 1–2 days ahead.  
- When bullish sentiment is high but true outcome is flat or falling, model overestimates momentum — reduce forecast by 1–3% per day for 3–5 days.  
- If supply net is negative and bullish sentiment is low, model often underestimates downside — add 2–4% buffer below forecast for 3–5 days.  
- If sentiment is bullish but true outcome is flat or falling, model overestimates momentum — reduce forecast by 1–3% per day for 3–5 days.  
- If sentiment is bearish but true outcome is rising, model underestimates upside — add 1–3% buffer above forecast for 3–5 days.  
- If sentiment is neutral or mixed, model tends to overfit recent trends — apply 50% smoothing to forecast to avoid overreaction.
